title: The four types of BOAT platform: Why regulated work needs process orchestration
summary: Explore the four types of BOAT platforms and why orchestration, governance, and process matter when scaling agentic automation.
body_markdown:
On paper, most enterprise automation platforms now advertise the same capabilities:[workflow orchestration](https://www.pega.com/workflow-orchestration) , integration,[robotic process automation](https://www.pega.com/robotic-process-automation) , low-code development, and AI agent building. That convergence is exactly what makes platform selection harder, not easier. A feature-by-feature checklist hides the differences that actually matter, and those differences only surface once agentic automation moves out of a pilot and into a regulated process, a customer journey, or a core operation, where a wrong decision has consequences.


In our opinion Gartner® makes this point directly in its research note *Choosing the Right BOAT for Agentic Automation* . Despite feature convergence,[business orchestration and automation technology (BOAT)](https://www.pega.com/business-orchestration-automation-technologies) platforms differ significantly in how they handle agent coordination, process durability, governance, observability, connectivity, and runtime control. We feel Gartner notes that those differences become material the moment agentic automation leaves the pilot stage and starts touching work the business actually depends on.¹ Gartner also reframes the buying question itself: The key selection question is no longer simply, “Which platform automates the most tasks?” It is, “Which platform can safely coordinate agentic work when reasoning, tools, data, humans, and process state must come together under enterprise control?”¹


## Gartner's four types of BOAT platform


Gartner groups BOAT platforms into four types, each shaped by the market it grew out of, and cautions that treating BOAT as a single, uniform category leads organizations to buy for last decade's problems rather than for an agentic future.¹


Enterprise low-code automation platforms are built for breadth. Per Gartner, they provide broad BOAT capability coverage across workflow orchestration, integration, RPA, low-code development, and governance and operational management. These platforms prioritize consolidation, centralized governance, and enterprise-scale execution. Typical strengths include: natural language-based AI agent building, CLI integration like Claude and OpenClaw, and multiagent coordination.¹


Supporting agent reasoning patterns, BPM and BPA process orchestration specialists are built for depth. Gartner describes them as platforms that emphasize deep[process orchestration](https://www.pega.com/process-orchestration) ,[case management](https://www.pega.com/case-management) , and long-running workflow coordination. Although most of these platforms are geared toward agentic automation, they prioritize heavy deterministic processes over nondeterministic actions. Typical strengths include: Strong BPMN and decision-modeling support, long-running and event-driven orchestration, advanced case management, and exception handling ¹


Integration-centric platforms’ approach is primarily through APIs, MCPs, events, runtime connectivity, and orchestration fabrics. These platforms increasingly position themselves as lightweight orchestration and coordination layers for distributed automation and AI ecosystems. Typical strengths include: API-first orchestration, event-driven coordination, and MCP and agent connectivity BOAT through APIs, events, and runtime connectivity. This helps position themselves as lightweight coordination layers for distributed automation and AI ecosystems. Gartner rates them strong on interoperability and composability, and optimized for integration-led strategies rather than deep[workflow management](https://www.pega.com/workflow-management) or durable orchestration.¹


AI agent specialists approach BOAT from an AI-first perspective, prioritizing agent development, model orchestration, LLM runtimes, and rapid experimentation over deterministic process control. Typical strengths include: Excellence in reasoning, autonomy, and integration with broader AI ecosystems rather than structured, long-running process orchestration, AI agent development, and coordination ¹


## Which type fits regulated, mission-critical work


Gartner says choosing between these platform types is not primarily about vendor maturity or market leadership. It is a question of architectural fit, orchestration requirements, and enterprise operating model alignment. Organizations that align BOAT platform selection with long-term orchestration, governance, and AI agent control requirements will be better positioned to scale agentic automation sustainably while avoiding costly platform fragmentation and future realignment. ¹


For regulated, mission-critical operations, that ordering is the whole decision. Claims processing, KYC, prior authorization, and benefits determination are deterministic, long-running, exception-heavy processes that have to be governed and audited from start to finish. In that world, process orchestration and[governance](https://www.pega.com/ai-governance) are the capabilities that matter most, and agent breadth comes second. A platform that indexes on multiagent experimentation at the expense of durable, auditable orchestration is optimized for the opposite problem.


## Where Pega fits


Gartner named Pega among the BPM/BPA process orchestration specialists,¹ and we think the fit traces to specific architectural decisions rather than a feature list.


## Predictable outcomes, by architecture


[Pega](https://www.pega.com/) runs workflows, case management,[real-time decisioning](https://www.pega.com/real-time-decisioning) , and AI on a single rules-driven runtime, so there's no cross-engine synchronization to get wrong and governance stays consistent across every kind of automation. Case instances persist in Pega's own relational database across their full lifecycle with no enforced timeout, which is what lets a claim or a months-long investigation stay intact and auditable rather than losing state at a system boundary. A[real-time decision engine](https://www.pega.com/decisioning-engines) sits inside the case lifecycle itself, adapting how work is routed based on predictive models, contextual data, and business rules without depending on a large language model for that runtime reasoning, which keeps the decision path deterministic and explainable even as AI is layered in. These are the capabilities that make Pega a fit for highly regulated environments, backed by certifications including FedRAMP High, HIPAA, and PCI DSS, across its top industries in financial services, insurance, and telecommunications.


## Reimagining processes for the AI era


Depth of orchestration is only useful if you can design against it quickly.[Pega Blueprint](https://www.pega.com/blueprint) turns natural-language requirements and existing legacy assets into executable process and application designs, accelerating discovery and design and cutting the manual effort of modernizing complex processes. For regulated operations still running on decades-old systems, that's the difference between automating a broken process and reimagining it for the AI era before automating it.


## Predictable costs


Plenty of IT projects never show a clear, positive return, and pricing is part of why. Most platform vendors measure usage across a sprawl of consumption units that are hard to predict and, worse, aren't tied to whether any actual work got done. Token-based AI pricing makes it sharper, since token consumption rises and falls with how hard a model happens to reason on a given run. Pega takes the opposite approach with case-based licensing. A case is a unit of work carried from start to completion, so you pay for outcomes rather than activity, and the price is tied to value delivered rather than to how much the system had to churn to get there. A case includes unlimited use of whatever capability the work requires, which takes the runaway-cost risk of per-token pricing off the table.


## Match the platform to the process


Gartner guidance is to choose by architectural fit and operating model, not by market recognition alone.¹ To us, paraphrased for the decision at hand: Choose an enterprise low-code platform when broad agent building matters more than process-orchestration depth; an integration-centric platform when interoperability and event coordination across distributed services matters most and tasks are moderate in complexity; an AI agent specialist when reasoning, agent collaboration, and rapid experimentation are the priority; and a process orchestration specialist when you need deep, durable, auditable orchestration of long-running, exception-heavy work with AI agents inside the guardrails. For regulated, mission-critical operations, evaluate on how well a platform handles exceptions and holds a durable, traceable process together, not on how many agents it can spin up in a demo.
